content: Breast engorgement occurs when an excessive amount of breast milk accumulates in the mammary glands. This condition is often caused by insufficient breastfeeding or blocked milk ducts. When the breasts become engorged, they may swell, throb, and cause pain that can range from mild to severe. If left untreated, engorgement can lead to mastitis, which is an inflammation of the breast tissue. Women experiencing this may notice a lump in a specific area of the breast, and the skin over that area may appear red and feel warm to the touch. If the plugged duct is not addressed, it can progress to a breast infection, which may present with symptoms such as fever or flu-like sensations. To manage breast engorgement, it is crucial to continue breastfeeding rather than reducing it, as frequent nursing helps to decrease milk levels and prevent further complications. Treatment for engorgement, plugged ducts, and infections involves frequent nursing to facilitate milk drainage. Applying wet heat and performing gentle massage on the affected areas of the breast, directing the motion toward the nipple, can be beneficial before nursing. Additionally, positioning the baby so that their chin points toward the most affected area of the breast can help clear the blockage. If the condition progresses to mastitis, it is important to maintain adequate nutrition and hydration. Bed rest and frequent nursing, ensuring no more than two hours pass between the start of one feeding and the next, are essential. If a breast infection is not treated or is inadequately managed, it can develop into a breast abscess, which may require surgical drainage. Any breast infection that persists for more than 24 hours or becomes severe should be promptly reported to a healthcare provider, as antibiotic therapy may be necessary. It is also important to note that a rare but serious condition called inflammatory breast cancer can present with symptoms similar to mastitis, such as breast swelling. This type of cancer has been reported in breastfeeding women and is the most aggressive form of breast cancer, with the highest mortality rate. It is often not detectable through mammography or ultrasound. If mastitis or a breast abscess does not improve after two weeks of antibiotic treatment, the possibility of inflammatory breast cancer should be investigated by a physician.
